transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-18 15:00 PDT
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Alex Martin (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Michael Liu (Omega - Head of ML Infra), Sara Gomez (Omega - SRE), Tom Becker (Omega - CTO)

Summary: Quick deep-dive on KV cache eviction issues we've been seeing in prod where long-context sessions cause sporadic latency spikes and apparent "cold misses" after idle periods.

[00:00] Alex Martin: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll keep this to about 55 minutes, we wanted to walk through the KV cache behavior you reported and get to the root cause - quick intros?
[00:12] Michael Liu: yeah, thanks. I can give context. We're running a private deployment in our VPC, 8xA10 Gpus, mostly 32k seq models for chat, we've seen periodic token-latency spikes where the tail p95 jumps from 120ms to 800ms for a few minutes even though throughput is steady.
[00:30] Priya Desai: thanks, mike. Couple quick clarifying q's - when you see the spikes is it across all users or just a subset, and do you have any correlation with large requests or model version switches?
[00:42] Michael Liu: it's kinda subset, usually threads that are using very long context or reusing very long prefixes. not model switches. we also noticed it after idle bursts, like after a quiet period a specific conv gets slow.
[01:05] Priya Desai: ok that smells like eviction + prefix cold misses. our KV cache is per-shard LRU-ish with segmented hot lists; but on heavy long-context the stored KV can grow and trigger aggressive eviction to keep working set bounded, and then a later request re-creates the kv entries which looks like a cold fill and increases latency.
[01:25] Tom Becker: can you explain the "segmented hot list" - we saw mem usage drop then spike, is that the same thing?
[01:34] Priya Desai: yeah, so we maintain a hot set for recently used prefixes and a cold set for older ones. eviction policy is roughly LRU with some heuristics - we also have an approximate clock algorithm to avoid global locks. but the seg lists can fragment, and when we compact or re-balance there's a short pause while metadata is updated, it's normally tiny but can be amplified under contention or big batch sizes.
[02:05] Sara Gomez: also we're using aggressive batching at the router layer, could batching be causing extra memory pressure?
[02:12] Priya Desai: absolutely - batching increases peak KV memory because multiple requests hold references to KV simultaneously; so instead of one active seq you can have 8x or more. if your seq lengths are long that multiplies the working set.
[02:30] Alex Martin: just to add, quantization affects per-token compute but also slightly changes kv sizes when using some kernel paths - low-bit kernels may pack keys differently which can change memory footprint, we have seen that change eviction thresholds by 5-10%.
[02:50] Michael Liu: interesting. we are on 4-bit quantized weights for the model. how do we know if the eviction is the direct cause and not garbage collection on host or swap/paging at OS?
[03:05] Priya Desai: good call, we should check both sides. steps: collect per-gpu memory histograms, KV cache hit/miss counters, eviction events, and host dmesg/syslog for oom_killer or pageouts. also collect process pprof while reproducing.
[03:28] Alex Martin: can you share your sequence length distribution, and the set of hot prefixes you expect to be reused? that will help us reproduce locally and calibrate the working set.
[03:38] Michael Liu: yes we'll share distribution and the top ~50 prefixes used by our chat UI.
[03:45] Priya Desai: we should also check sharding: if the KV is sharded across GPUs, prefix reuse across shards will not hit the local cache and will force remote fetch or re-computation. are you pinning prefixes to particular shards?
[03:58] Michael Liu: i don't think we have strong pinning, it's mostly router-based modulo sharding.
[04:05] Priya Desai: that's likely part of it - lack of affinity increases churn. options: increase shard affinity for long sessions, or switch to a shared KV plane with faster interconnects (RDMA) or maintain a global index to reduce duplication.
[04:25] Tom Becker: RDMA isn't an option in our VPC yet. what about paging - could you page older kv to host RAM or NVMe?
[04:34] Priya Desai: we do have an experimental paging layer that writes cold KV segments to NVMe with async prefetch; however the latency cost for a miss is large - 10-50ms depending on NVMe and PCIe saturation - and we only enable it for customers who accept slightly higher tail. It can help stabilise memory pressure but doesn't eliminate cold fill latency.
[05:05] Alex Martin: also worth noting there's an implementation detail: when the KV page is paged to disk and then reloaded, we currently do a metadata revalidation step that can take extra cycles under lock contention - we can share a patch that reduces that.
[05:20] Sara Gomez: in our logs we saw a pattern: eviction events spike right before the latency bursts, then fill events spike. can you explain what causes that timing?
[05:30] Priya Desai: usually that's a combination of a burst of new sessions (e.g., morning wave) + a scheduled background task that cleans and compacts segments. if compaction happens right when working set grows, you get a temporary eviction wave. compaction is opportunistic but we can tune the threshold.
[05:55] Michael Liu: is there a recommended config for long context workloads?
[06:02] Priya Desai: yes: increase cache size calibrations (if you have spare GPU memory), increase hot list threshold so items are promoted more aggressively, and reduce aggressive compaction frequency. Also set router to prefer affinity for long sessions.
[06:20] Alex Martin: we can provide a config snippet - we'll attach to the follow-up.
[06:27] Tom Becker: what telemetry should we enable right away so we can triage faster?
[06:33] Priya Desai: enable per-request kv_hit kv_miss counters, eviction_count, current_working_set_bytes, per-shard mem usage, and a histogram of seq length per request. Increase sampling for pprof traces around high-latency requests. Also collect kernel-level page faults and dmesg.
[07:00] Michael Liu: our retention window for traces is short - will those metrics be heavy on overhead?
[07:07] Alex Martin: counters are cheap; pprof sampling is small if done for short windows; we typically suggest 5s captures around incidents.
[07:15] Priya Desai: one more gotcha: token streaming with small chunk sizes can cause the runtime to refill KV frequently because each chunk may trigger small partial state updates. batching and chunking settings interact with KV lifetime.
[07:35] Sara Gomez: ours uses 4-token streaming chunks. could that be too small?
[07:40] Priya Desai: it could - bigger chunks reduce overhead but increase latency to first token. there's a balance. for high-throughput background jobs 16-32 token chunking is common; for interactive chat you might keep smaller chunking but tune cache lifetimes.
[07:58] Tom Becker: are there any immediate mitigations if we can't increase GPU RAM?
[08:03] Priya Desai: yes: 1) improve affinity so long sessions hit same shard; 2) enable selective pinning of hot prefixes; 3) tune router to avoid mixing heavy long-context with short-context in same batch; 4) enable NVMe paging in exchange for higher tail; 5) reduce batching maximums temporarily during incidents.
[08:30] Alex Martin: priya, can you walk through what logs we should pull?
[08:34] Priya Desai: sure - per-gpu free_mem timeline, kv_evict events with keys (hashed), kv_fill durations, per-request seq_len, batch sizes, router decisions (shard id), and pprof cpu/gpu traces. Also include any host swap/pageouts.
[08:55] Michael Liu: i'll get ops to collect those and drop them in the shared s3 bucket.
[09:00] Priya Desai: another possible root cause: fragmentation in CX cache allocator. If we have many small allocations from varying seq lengths, fragmentation can lead to apparent free memory but unusable for large contiguous KV entries, causing evictions. allocator stats will help.
[09:20] Sara Gomez: do you have tooling to visualize fragmentation?
[09:24] Priya Desai: we have internal allocator dumps, we'll share a parser script that outputs free spans and fragmentation ratio.
[09:30] Tom Becker: any changes to quantization we should try?
[09:35] Priya Desai: switching quantization modes sometimes increases or decreases kv footprint; for example, 4-bit symmetric vs 4-bit per-channel packings differ. we can test both; keep an eye on per-token memory use.
[09:50] Michael Liu: are there known bugs that cause mass eviction?
[09:55] Priya Desai: there's a known corner where metadata version skew during rolling restarts can trigger global invalidation - rare but if you saw spikes coincident with deploys that might be it. otherwise it's config/sharding/memory pressure.
[10:12] Alex Martin: good - let's talk experiment plan. we'll run a repro with your seqlen distribution and hot prefixes, try three configs: baseline, affinity+pinning, and NVMe paging enabled. measure p50/p95 tail and eviction counts.
[10:30] Michael Liu: sounds good - timeline?
[10:33] Alex Martin: Priya will gather logs and run a bench this week; target bench next Tue (2025-06-24) and follow-up sync Wed.
[10:44] Priya Desai: i'll also include a lightweight patch that reduces metadata locking during page-in. it's safe but we want to pressure test it.
[11:00] Tom Becker: ok thanks. any last q's?
[11:05] Sara Gomez: none.
[11:08] Michael Liu: thanks everyone.
